newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electric futures end higher on SW strength.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electric futures end higher on SW strength.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures settled higher Tuesday on the strength of the cash market in the U.S. Southwest tied to tight supply and strong air-conditioning demand in the region.
"We were up on the cash," said a Houston futures trader, referring to a spike in physical values in the Southwest which spilled into the futures complex.
August Palo Verde (PV) futures settled up 35 cents at $35.45 a megawatt hour (MWh) after peaking at $36.10, just 15 cents below their life-of-contract high.
September PV finished up 27 cents at $29.53. Other PV contracts ended down five to up 30 cents.
August California-Oregon Border (COB) settled up eight cents at $23.24 after bouncing between $23.05 and $23.60.
September COB finished up seven cents at $22.95. Deferred COB months ended down five to up 10 cents.
Southwest spot power prices surged today on real-time transmission constraint on the Pacific Intertie as well as triple-digit heat in interior cities such as Phoenix and Tuscon, market sources said.
Day-ahead electricity prices for Wednesday at PV leaped to six to seven dollars to $38.00-41.00 while those at COB rose just 50 cents to $17.50-18.50.

Strength in the Southwest power market was also underpinned by a unplanned outage of the 750 megawatt (MW) Mohave coal-fired unit 2 in Nevada and a delay in restarting one of the San Onofre nuclear power unit in California.
The Mohave unit which tripped off line yesterday due to a tube leak was set to resume operation late Wednesday.

Southern California Edison (SoCal Edison) decided to postpone the restart of the 1,080 MW unit 3 at its San Onofre station to July 17 from July 10. Engineers needed time to replace the unit's instrument nozzles.
The San Onofre unit, in San Clemente, Calif., has been offline since April 12 for refueling and maintenance.
SoCal Edison added the adjacent 1,080 MW unit 2 was still on schedule to return to service near July 10 after being shut June 29 to replace charge line check valves.
Despite the ongoing outages of the above units, two large nuclear power plants were ramping up toward full output.
The 1,073 MW unit 2 at the Diablo Canyon nuclear power plant on the central California coast was expected to reach full power by this evening, PG&E Corp said.
The 1,158 MW WNP-2 nuclear power plant in Washington state hit 15 percent power early today but had not yet reconnected to the electricity grid.
Brokers and traders said they are uncertain about the direction for power complex.
"People are looking for sure direction. People are insecure about what to do," a West Coast broker said.

Although futures prices appear overvalued with the spate of nuclear generation set to come back in the next two weeks, players are reluctant to sell due to boom in Southwest cash prices, brokers and traders said.
Wet and cool weather was expected in the Pacific Northwest into the weekend before a warming trend was forecast for early next week.
Temperatures were projected to average near normal over most of the Southwest but below normal in the far northeast region and above normal in the extreme southwest area.
((--R Leong, New York Power Desk +1 212 859 1622))
